cover_letter.recipient:
Application Security Product team, Cloudflare
Re: Senior Product Manager, Zero-Day Protection
paragraphs: Cloudflare's WAF changelog this autumn shows where the hard part of zero-day protection now sits. The Brotli rules on 25 October and the Java4Shell detections on 18 November shipped in Log mode to limit false-positive risk, which leaves each customer to decide when protection becomes enforcement. Helping customers make that call quickly and safely is the work I would most like to own, and it is why I am applying for this role.

It is a problem I recognise. I own production LLM products for a top-10 US biopharmaceutical company, where an output that breaks a compliance rule is an incident, not a bug. When a senior stakeholder asked how we knew the system was safe, I went through the workflow agent by agent, separating what must never vary, such as approved claims and templates, from the decisions where model variance had to be measured. That became a matrix of 60 tests across retrieval, agent decisions, end-to-end flow and safety, including prompt-injection and red-team cases.

Just as much of my work is making the system legible. I made explainability a product standard so compliance reviewers can see why each output was produced, and gave every agent its own metrics, including false-positive and false-negative rates. When a library change put older templates at risk, I held the customer announcement until the risk was confirmed. Your customers need the same clarity: what protection they have, what an event means and what to do next.

I would also bring range. The product suite I lead earned USD 4M+ in licence revenue, I direct a 28+ person cross-functional delivery across four regions, and I lead two product managers and a business analyst. I work AI-first, and designed my team's product workflow around Claude.

The gap is real: I have not run a WAF or written detection rules, and my security depth comes from AI safety testing rather than HTTP exploitation. I started as a software engineer and still analyse raw API payloads myself, and I would lean on your Security Research team for threat context while bringing the product judgement.
Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome a conversation about how you think about the move from Log to Block, and where the zero-day experience goes next.

cover.title: Closing the Log-to-Block gap in zero-day protection
cover.subtitle: A product hypothesis for WAF Managed Rules, built from Cloudflare's public changelog

slides.title: Customers need evidence, not just rules, to enforce zero-day protection quickly
lines: Cloudflare shipped emergency WAF releases on **10 separate days** between 14 October and 24 November 2026.
Several new detections shipped in **Log mode or disabled**, to limit false-positive risk.
Each customer then decides alone when to switch to Block, just as exploitation can begin.
Hypothesis: show each customer how a rule behaves **on their own traffic** before they enforce it.
I have built this discipline for production LLM agents: prove behaviour, measure variance, then ship.
slides.source: Cloudflare WAF changelog, Oct–Nov 2026; Senior PM, Zero-Day Protection role description

slides.title: Emergency WAF rules now arrive on a near-weekly cadence across many frameworks
lines: Releases labelled Emergency on **10 separate days** from 14 October to 24 November 2026.
Coverage spans PHP, Ruby, WordPress, Java, Next.js, Nuxt and Brotli handling.
December 2025's React rule protected proxied free and paid customers automatically, Block by default.
The role's goal: protect **more than 20% of the Internet** from HTTP-exploitable vulnerabilities.
slides.so_what: Fast rule delivery is already a strength. The next gains sit after the rule ships.

slides.title: Many new rules ship in Log mode, so enforcement becomes the customer's decision
lines: Brotli and Next.js rules (25 Oct) defaulted to **Log**: they also match legitimate traffic.
Java4Shell (18 Nov) and PHP-FPM / SOAP (19 Nov) shipped in Log to limit false positives.
The Nuxt Image rule (30 Oct) shipped **disabled**, with partial coverage only.
In May 2026, some React and Next.js flaws could not be blocked safely by a global rule.
slides.so_what: The protection exists, but each customer must judge alone whether Block will break their application.
slides.source: WAF changelog entries of 25 Oct, 30 Oct, 18 Nov and 19 Nov 2026; changelog of 7 May 2026

slides.title: Make the Log-to-Block decision evidence-based, per customer and per rule
lines: **Exposure**: flag which of the customer's applications run the affected software.
**Evidence**: replay the rule's Log matches on the customer's own traffic and estimate false positives.
**Staged enforcement**: Block one host or path first, with automatic rollback triggers.
**Explanation**: every event states what matched, why, and the next action to take.
slides.so_what: Hypothesis to test: evidence per rule shortens time from Log to Block without raising false blocks.
slides.source: Proposal by Iman Sadhu from public information; not a description of Cloudflare's internal roadmap

slides.title: I have shipped this discipline for production LLM agents in a regulated industry
lines: Separated what must never vary from where variance is measured: **60 tests** in one matrix.
Per-agent metrics, including validator **false-positive and false-negative** rates, plus one end-to-end score.
Made explainability a product standard so compliance reviewers can verify every output.
Held a customer announcement until a release risk was confirmed.
slides.so_what: Same pattern, new domain: prove behaviour on real inputs, measure variance, then enforce.
slides.source: Iman Sadhu, Senior Product Manager, Indegene (Feb 2025 to present): GenAI content platform for global pharma

slides.title: My first 90 days would test this hypothesis with customers before building anything
lines: **Days 1–30**: shadow Security Research through live releases; interview Enterprise customers on Log-to-Block.
**Days 31–60**: measure time-to-Block and false-block rates for recent emergency rules, where data allows.
**Days 61–90**: prototype per-customer rule evidence with a design-partner cohort; agree success metrics.
slides.so_what: Start from data and customers; commit the roadmap once the evidence is in.
slides.source: Proposed plan; assumptions to validate with the team

close.title: Thank you
lines: Shipping the rule starts protection; giving customers the **confidence to enforce it** finishes the job.
I would bring evidence-first product discipline from shipping AI in a regulated industry.

open_items: KNOCKOUT CHECK: the listing says 'Remote within: US, Canada, UK, Portugal'. The profile lists Bangalore, with relocation open to Dubai, Malaysia and Malta. Confirm eligibility before applying.
Export control: an offer may depend on authorisation under US export laws without sponsorship. Check before investing more time.
Gap (R12): no WAF, managed-rules, detection-engineering or security-research evidence in the master file. The cover letter states this plainly; the resume does not claim it.

Resume: all 24 bullets are Fact; no G1/G2 lines were needed. KPI tiles 3 and 4 (60 tests, ~87% accuracy) were chosen because the role centres on testing before enforcement and false-positive management.
R10: ACH-011 and ACH-044 overlap; merged into one bullet that cites both.
CONFIRM-FIRST skipped: ACH-072 (red-team assessment, role to confirm). Red-team wording comes from ACH-044 instead.

Cover letter G1/G2 phrasing to confirm: 'an output that breaks a compliance rule is an incident, not a bug' (framing) and 'still analyse raw API payloads myself' (ACH-048 records two payloads analysed).
Deck: the Resolution slide is a hypothesis built from public changelog data, labelled as such; it makes no claim about Cloudflare's internal plans.
